entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John of Ragusa (born Ivan Stojković around 1390 in Dubrovnik, then the Republic of Ragusa) was a pivotal Croatian Dominican theologian, scholar, and diplomat whose career epitomized the tumultuous intellectual and ecclesiastical struggles of the 15th century. A staunch advocate for conciliarism, he rose to prominence as a leading voice at the Council of Basel, challenging papal supremacy and striving for church reform. His diplomatic missions, particularly to Constantinople, underscore the era's persistent efforts to reunite the Eastern and Western Christian traditions amidst the encroaching Ottoman threat.

After completing his theological studies at the Universities of Padua and Paris, where he earned his Master's degree in 1420 and served as Rector in 1425, John of Ragusa became a central figure at the Council of Basel, which convened in 1431. There, he delivered influential sermons and treatises, vigorously defending the council's authority over the Pope, particularly in his work "Libellus de ecclesiastica potestate et auctoritate concilii generalis." His most significant diplomatic undertaking was leading the Basle legation to Constantinople between 1435 and 1437, successfully inviting the Eastern Orthodox Church to participate in discussions for union.

Despite his efforts, the schism between the council and Pope Eugene IV ultimately led to the Council of Ferrara-Florence, which he did not support. His conciliarist stance aligned him with the anti-pope Felix V, who appointed him cardinal in 1440, a title never recognized by Rome. John of Ragusa's extensive collection of Greek manuscripts, acquired during his eastern travels, significantly enriched Western scholarship, transmitting invaluable classical and patristic texts. His theological and historical writings, including a comprehensive history of the Council of Basel, provide crucial primary source material for understanding the late medieval Church.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: John of Ragusa was a central figure in the conciliar movement, significantly shaping the theological and political debates surrounding papal authority in the 15th century. His diplomatic efforts to unite the Eastern and Western Churches and his transmission of Greek manuscripts left a lasting impact on both ecclesiastical history and Renaissance scholarship.
